entries.title: Allies & Enemies
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Blaming Canada. An exclusive look at a new report on voters known as “Trump Regretters.” The Pentagon’s money problems. A first look at ads attacking Medicare for All. Kalshi vs. regulators. Reality vs USPS ballot rules. And: A look at opportunity zones, eight years later.





THE LATEST

Drinking the anti-Canadian Club? The White House’s fight with America’s northern neighbor continues, trapping border-state Republicans in a conundrum: Do they join up with Donald Trump’s rhetorical crusade and set sail across Lake America looking for a fight? Or do they try to keep up a relationship with a longtime economic partner that is often crucial to a significant number of their constituents?

“I want to get the train back on the tracks. And I think we can do that,” Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Michigan) told NOTUS’ Manuela Silva this week — not exactly chastising Trump but not exactly praising him, either.

Another tough one for Republicans! Cross Trump and there could be political trouble from MAGA; join in the attacks on Canada and there could be political problems at home. “I’m not a big fan of the current situation because Indiana’s a big trading partner with Canada, so I prefer the issue go away,” Republican Rep. Mark Messmer said.

There were some Republicans eager to sign on to Trump’s approach to Canada: “I would hope NOTUS is going to say, ‘Thank you, President Trump, for finally leveling the playing field, taking care of our farmers,’” said Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan, the House Republican Conference chair.

“I stay out of all the back-and-forth,” Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-New York) said. She had plenty of complaints about Canadian trade practices — “so much dumping of powdered milks” — but she stressed that her strong relationships with Canadian lawmakers continue, and urged people not to get too anxious.

“Somehow, I think this shall pass,” she said. Barrett, McClain and Tenney, by the way, were at the Rose Garden dinner with Trump last night.

Could that anxiety create more “Trump Regretters” in the swing seats? Navigator Research, the Democratic-leaning messaging firm, is out with a big new report on this set of potential 2026 voters, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports. Using survey and focus-group findings, the firm digs in on Trump 2024 supporters who have hung up their red hats. “One-in-five 2024 Trump voters now regret their vote, especially younger Americans, Black and Latino Americans, independents or non-MAGA Republicans, and moms,” the report finds. “Rising costs and expensive wars among top reasons why Trump voters now regret their vote.”

More on NOTUS: ‘Darn Unusual’ DOJ Filing Has the Trump Administration on Different Path | Strategists Say Battleground Democrats Won’t Be Able to Easily Shake ‘Woke 1.0’ | Federal Judge Blocks Trump’s Latest Effort to Restrict Birthright Citizenship





From the Pentagon


Cash crunch: The stopgap funding bill the House passed to keep the government open through the midterms does not provide the tens of billions of dollars the Pentagon says it needs to cover Iran operations, replenish munitions and sustain forces whose deployments have been extended. NOTUS’ Joe Gould and Avani Kalra report on how some observers see the budget moving forward: There’s a narrow window (like three weeks) for another reconciliation bill to be passed by the Republicans in both chambers. Barring that, the DOD is going to have to figure out how to stretch pennies until after the election.

From the campaign trail


First on NOTUS: Republicans run against “Medicare for All.” A new six-figure ad buy is launching today in D.C. from Seniors Matter for America, a group connected to Trump 1.0 press secretary Sean Spicer. The ads take aim at Democratic candidates over the signature health care proposal backed by progressives, which the group calls “pushing everyone into one government system run by federal bureaucrats.” What you’ll be hearing: “Seniors will show up in November, and the choice couldn’t be more clear: The Republicans fighting for their benefits or the Democrats destroying them?”

More: FEC to Klobuchar: Explain Your $42,000 ‘Asset Transfer’ Between Campaigns | Elon Musk’s Super PAC Dumped $800K Into Battleground Races in August

From K Street


More like K-alshi Street: The prediction market company now has over two-dozen federal lobbyists working on its behalf, including some heavy hitters from across the political spectrum — former Democratic Sen. Blanche Lincoln is one, veteran Republican cloakroom staffer Tony Hanagan is another. As NOTUS’ Mark Alfred reports, this army of influence is up against a growing tide of pro-regulation electeds — and so far, the potential regulations are languishing.

More: New Jersey Takes Its Fight Against Kalshi to the Supreme Court

From the Hill


First on NOTUS: Taking on detention centers. Rep. Veronica Escobar (D-Texas) is introducing legislation that would put new requirements on DHS before it can establish new detention facilities, just weeks after the department scrapped a plan to convert a warehouse in her district to hold immigrants. Some of the requirements the legislation would impose: consulting with local officials, holding public meetings and analyzing potential resource strain.

More: Russia Sanctions Bill Remains Stalled Despite Pressure From Zelenskyy’s Top Envoy

From the White House


Special guest: The White House announced Vice President JD Vance will brief reporters today, filling the void as temporary press secretary for the day. It will be the first briefing since July 23.

Ring ring: Trump debuted a new phone on the Resolute Desk, trimmed in gold, of course. The White House didn’t respond to questions about where it came from or who designed the new device. And neither did Cisco, whose name adorns the top. Don’t confuse the new desk phone with the other gold Trump Phone, which didn’t work out so well.

More: Trump Says White House Helipad Is Complete | Trump Is Planning a Midterm Travel Blitz to Alaska and Other Battlegrounds





THE BIG ONE

One part of the new USPS mail-ballot rule is so time consuming that it’s all but impossible, election officials and experts say. NOTUS’ Eric Katz and Adora Brown report on the various timelines local officials have said it would take to send outgoing mail ballots as required under the new rules — 66,000 hours, or more than seven years, of staff time in Colorado; between 25,000 and 50,000 hours in Oregon.

“It would take about 4.9 years of continuous scanning to verify the whole mailing,” said Tammy Patrick, a former federal compliance officer for elections in Maricopa County, Arizona.

Inside the USPS, some are not feeling much more confident. While the USPS requirements mark a completely new procedure for the agency, postmasters who run the facilities that will receive ballots have yet to be given any guidance for carrying them out, a senior Postal Service source told NOTUS.

A federal court has temporarily blocked the new rules and a number of states continue to push back against them.





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

The hundreds of millions of books the late, great Dolly Parton gave to kids wasn’t just an impressive act of charity, writes NOTUS’ Kainaz Amaria. It created a common reading list in a society that desperately needs one.

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: Plane Carrying DHS Secretary Makes Emergency Landing at DCA, by Kendall Staton

Talk to Tom: Where to Go for a Celebratory Dinner, by Tom Sietsema





NEW ON NOTUS

Missed opportunity? “This is the first I’ve heard about this program,” a rural county treasurer in Illinois told NOTUS’ Jade Lozada about opportunity zones. It’s been eight years since the federal government began a tax-incentive program, dubbed “opportunity zones,” aimed at attracting economic development in low-income areas across the country. As the Treasury Department fields nominations for a second round of the program, Jade looks at where it’s worked (hint: bigger cities) and it hasn’t (rural areas).

entries.title: Are ‘Opportunity Zones’ Creating Opportunity? Rural America Is Waiting.
entries.summary: Local officials tell NOTUS they haven’t seen investment dollars pour in. But they’re welcoming the coming changes to the tax program.
entries.content:
Montgomery County, Illinois, is roughly 700 square miles of sparsely populated land almost perfectly situated in between Springfield and St. Louis. It’s home to a Route 66 Welcome Center and, if a federal tax-incentive program is successful, is supposed to be a hotspot for new economic development.

But when Mike Plunkett, a county coordinator whose job it is to field those millions of dollars in investment, looks around, he wonders why a developer would come there.

“What do we have to offer that a million other Midwestern communities don’t have? We have very little competitive advantage,” Plunkett said.

In the eight years since the federal government implemented “opportunity zones,” a tax-incentive program that aims to spur economic development in selected low-income census tracts in the U.S., many counties have been experiencing what Montgomery has.

As the Treasury Department fields nominations from governors’ offices for the second round of opportunity zone investments this summer — tracts that will be eligible for tax-incentivized investments starting in January 2027 — communities are wondering whether they will actually experience the benefits of the program this time.

Plunkett said he has received only one inquiry about the program: from a construction gear manufacturer that set up shop in Montgomery County.

“There have been no other inquiries about the opportunity zone,” Plunkett added.

Multiple local officials from around the country reached by NOTUS said they weren’t aware their county was in an opportunity zone. “This is the first I’ve heard about this program,” said a rural county treasurer in Illinois, who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation. “There isn’t any attraction to come here.”

The average rural zone attracted just $7.3 million in investment from 2018 to 2024, compared to $23.3 million for the average nonrural opportunity zone, according to a June paper by the Treasury’s Office of Tax Analysis. In total, 16% of opportunity zone property was in rural areas, even though it makes up 38% of the U.S.’s 8,764 opportunity zones. In all, $112 billion has been invested using opportunity zone tax incentives.

There’s no comprehensive federal tracking of the impact of opportunity zones, but outside research has shown the program yielding mixed results. Opportunity zones have spurred the construction of 416,000 new homes, according to one paper from the Economic Innovation Group, a think tank that leads the pack in measuring the program’s impact. They have created new jobs, most of which go to residents from more affluent areas outside of the opportunity zone, reports another from the National Bureau of Economic Research. They have no significant effect on commercial investment and business activity, says a third by economists Naomi Feldman and Kevin Corinth, who is a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

Local economic development officials largely said they felt the incentives were not properly promoted.

Corey Proctor, the planning director for Forrest County, Mississippi, said his county needs new housing and has vast swathes of land he believes could attract industry, but local developers lack the requisite information to leverage the tax incentive.

Those developers could benefit from workshops that provide a rundown on how to invest in an opportunity zone, whether delivered by his office or the state or federal government, Proctor said.

“It’d be good to have everyone on the same page,” he said.

Last year’s budget reconciliation law does seek to remedy the rural investment disparity.

Opportunity zones allow taxpayers to invest capital gains income from stocks or property into funds that back development projects in low-income tracts. In return, investors can defer and reduce their tax payments on their gains. After 10 years invested in the fund, gains on the opportunity zone investment itself are completely tax free.

Starting next year, investors in newly created rural opportunity zone funds will receive a 30% reduction in their capital gains tax bill after five years invested in a rural opportunity zone, compared to 10% for nonrural zones.

Rural counties can’t offer the scores of people to fill shiny new apartment complexes and office buildings, or the transit infrastructure to support construction that their urban competitors for opportunity zone dollars can. They also typically lack the robust economic development teams with arsenals of resources for investors to utilize that many cities leverage.

That puts rural counties in a tough spot. With limited county staff and few established local investors, rural county leaders said attracting opportunity zone investment will require an unprecedented effort by local economic planners to read up on opportunity zones and pitch their own to developers — work that they currently don’t do or don’t know about.

Local officials told NOTUS that having extensive data on the impact of opportunity zone investments could help draw in new investors.

Currently, no one — neither the developers, nor the opportunity zone municipalities or the Treasury Department — bears the explicit responsibility to measure the program’s impact before changes in last year’s budget reconciliation law. Investors currently need only submit basic data on the value and the location of their property holdings on annual tax forms.

Under the latest budget law, however, investors must report the numbers of residential units held and full-time workers employed in the fund’s businesses, as well as the basic data on their investments. Congress allocated $15 million for the Treasury to produce annual reports enumerating opportunity zones’ housing and job creation, as well as less-frequent reports detailing the impact of investment on metrics such as poverty and unemployment rates and median family income.

“That would be on my wishlist for opportunity zone 2.0 is to really strengthen the reporting mechanisms so that communities truly can major those ROIs,” said Kersten Swinyard, the economic development director for Salt Lake County, Utah. “We’d love to be able to highlight these numbers. We just don’t have them.”

Localities that have successfully drawn investment do not have a clear picture of the program’s impact — or take pains to estimate it. Though she lacked impact data, Swinyard said opportunity zones were an undeniable success in Salt Lake County, where the tax incentive helped attract large logistics and industrial projects, as well as housing and commercial development.

“Opportunity zones can be either a useful way to channel investment to places that really need it or a tax shelter with high abuse potential, and the determining factor as to which side wins out is precisely the type of tracking and evaluation that is required, and that we've never seen quite enough of,” said Jared Bernstein, the chief economic adviser to then-President Joe Biden who co-authored the original 2015 paper proposing opportunity zones with Kevin Hassett, the current National Economic Council director.

The program’s impact is hard to grasp even on the ground and even in urban areas with more resources.

In Washington, D.C., which has raked in $1.2 billion in opportunity zone investment, the mayor’s office and developers are trying their own hands at data-gathering to paint a picture of the program that will keep investors coming back.

The mayor’s office cobbles together assessments through its building permitting process, conversations with developers about how much capital they’ve deployed and job estimates configured by the city’s tax revenue and licensing offices, said Nina Albert, the deputy mayor for economic planning and development.

RedBrick LMD, one of the largest private landowners in D.C., has hired a third-party firm to evaluate their opportunity zone investments for the purpose of pitching to impact investors.

Opportunity zone projects like those of RedBrick have transformed pockets of the city, particularly in Anacostia, Congress Heights and Barry Farm.

Aside a bend in the Anacostia River, facing the white arches of the Frederick Douglass Memorial Bridge stretching to Navy Yard, RedBrick erected the Bridge District towers — a swanky mixed-income and mixed-use development with a plant wall in the lobby and a pool on the rooftop. A brewery and coffee shop sit on the ground floor.

The Bridge District — an opportunity zone project touted by Albert — went up in an area with little else, as the program intended. Bounded on one side by the river and treetops of Anacostia Park and the other by crisscrossing roadways, the closest major development visible from the roof is the Marine One hangar about two miles away.

Albert credits D.C.’s expansive tax incentives for developers beyond opportunity zones. There’s the federal New Markets Tax Credit Program, the District’s low-income-housing tax credit, and even a local tax incentive for opening grocery stores.

“It's surpassed our expectations,” Albert said of opportunity zones. “I wouldn't say it's our premier tool.”

RedBrick LMD managing partner Louis Dubin had a different take.

“Anything we may have done locally would be so de minimis it would really not have materially contributed. So I would attribute this all to opportunity zone,” the real-estate developer told NOTUS.

entries.title: Lutnick Apologizes for Saying No U.S. Troops Have Died in the Iran War
entries.summary: He claimed to have “misspoke” after confusing the conflict with another U.S. operation in Venezuela.
entries.content:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick apologized Thursday for saying in an interview that no American service members have died supporting military operations in Iran, claiming that he “misspoke” and accidentally conflated the conflict with another U.S. operation in Venezuela.

Lutnick incorrectly stated the death toll during a CNBC appearance Wednesday, saying, “The way the president is playing Iran — there haven't been American deaths, it's really just an economic choke out.”

At least 18 service members have died and more than 400 troops have been wounded in action as the military campaign in Iran stretches into six months with no clear end in sight. The Pentagon has reclassified the deaths of four service members, all of whom were killed during an Iranian ballistic missile attack in Jordan in late July, as part of “overseas operations” instead of Operation Epic Fury, the military’s name for the initial conflict with Iran.

Lutnick clarified in a post to X Thursday he was thinking about the military operation in January to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, which reportedly injured seven American troops and killed about 100 Venezuelans.

“18 members of our military have died, and to those families my heart breaks and I am so very sorry for their loss,” Lutnick wrote of the Iran war. “As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches, I am deeply thankful for our military and the sacrifices the men and women who serve our great country make, so such an attack, where I lost my brother Gary (36), my best friend Doug (39) and 656 other close friends and colleagues in the attacks on the World Trade Center, never happens again. Never!”

President Donald Trump also issued a clarification on Lutnick’s behalf Thursday.

“Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “18 people were killed in Iran!”

entries.title: Trump Says He’s Reconsidering His Support for UK Control Over the Falkland Islands
entries.summary: The president suggested that the UK’s lack of assistance during his war with Iran has made him think twice about supporting Britain’s claim to the territory.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump hinted on Thursday that he is reconsidering U.S. support for the U.K.’s claim to the Falkland Islands because of the country’s lack of support for his war against Iran.

Trump told British news channel GB News that Washington might not back the U.K. if Argentina were to invade the islands.

“Your country was not there to help me,” Trump said in a clip of the interview released on Thursday, referencing his frustration over Britain’s refusal to back U.S. military operations in Iran.

The U.S. has historically been neutral in the conflict, although Washington supported Britain’s campaign to control the Islands following an invasion by Argentina in 1982. In a 2013 referendum, residents voted 99.8% to remain a British overseas territory.

Trump’s comments come after Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has a close relationship with Trump, has launched an effort to claim control of the islands, restarting a long-standing dispute with the U.K. over the territory.

“The Malvinas were, are, and will always be Argentine,” Milei wrote on X in April.

Trump has repeatedly signaled his frustration with England and NATO for a lack of support in his ongoing war in Iran.

In the interview, Trump maintained that the U.K. is “not doing very well” and suggested the country had been weakened by repeated closures of the Strait of Hormuz. He argued the U.K. is “not the same country it was” when it initially won control over the Falkland Islands.

“I asked your former leader, ‘Why didn't you send a couple of ships?’” Trump said of the U.K.’s response to his war against Iran. “He said we don't have any, and it was pretty sad, the whole thing. So NATO was not there, even though most of those countries get a big portion of their oil from there.”

Trump also told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that the United States was reviewing its position on the islands. Those comments followed reporting by The Daily Telegraph that the Pentagon was reviewing the U.S. position on the islands in order to incentivize its NATO allies to up their defense spending commitments.

“I always review every position,” Trump said. “That’s just one of many.

entries.title: A Nationals Homestand Full of Agony and Hope
entries.summary: When a team becomes competitive again, as the Nats have, baseball regains its power to please.
entries.content:
The Washington Nationals homestand, just completed, illustrates in miniature a baseball fan’s experiences over a lifetime.

The Nats are roughly a .500 team. That’s the talent level you’d expect if you were a fan from age 6 to 96. But, for 10 straight days, every game at Nats Park was experienced by ardent fans as either a joyous 1.000, full of promise, or an abysmal .000 that, at least for a while, feels almost unendurable.

On some recent days, fans could hardly get higher about their team’s future. On some days, often the next day, they could hardly feel worse.

During this fortnight, the Nats won a game 13-3. Laughers are fun. They also got a walk-off win on a Dylan Crews hit. Drama works nicely, too.

Daylen Lile won National League Player of the Week, then hit two more homers to start his next week —14 RBIs in eight games! Cade Cavalli, the team's new ace, had his ninth straight quality start, second-most in team history after only Max Scherzer’s streak in 2019.

On Tuesday, rookies Yoyo Morales and Jared Simpson were the hitting hero and winning pitcher on their first day in the majors. The Morales and Simpson families were sitting together in Nats Park. Morales had a homer, a long double and a single. Simpson got nine outs on the eight batters that he faced. The moms and dads hardly knew who to high-five next.

My favorite feel-good of the season is now lefty reliever Erik Tolman, who touched 100 mph with a 0.00 ERA in his first four Nats games after five years of misfortunes that’d make Job feel lucky by comparison. Two Tommy John surgeries were his little injuries.

In the minors in ’23, making his second TJ comeback, Tolman hopped over the foul line for luck, but caught his cleat and fell awkwardly.

“I tore every ligament in my [right] knee, [my] hamstring tore off my bone, and then the peroneal nerve ruptured,” said Tolman in a TV interview. “I lost all feeling in my foot, which resulted in a foot drop.”

Tolman had to learn how to walk again. He now pitches with a brace on his lower leg and, when barefoot, still doesn’t have full feeling in his foot. But his fastball sits at 96-to-99. On a foul pop up, Tolman made an acrobatic twisting snag, reaching backward over his head. Did somebody say the Nats needed a left-handed reliever more than any other one thing?

So, top that! What can go wrong?

Plenty. Baseball gives you a day to enjoy a Tolman, or a seven-inning, one-run 106-pitch outing by another southpaw rookie, Jackson Kent. But you also get just one day to rehab from the ugliest losses.

On Sunday, the Nats bullpen turned a 2-0 lead in the ninth into a 6-2 loss. The gruesome way that they did it shows why baseball fans deserve medals. Miami took a 4-2 lead on a bunt single, three walks, a hit batter, two double steals (one of home plate), a wild outfield throw on a sacrifice fly and multiple mental errors. The Marlins’ only “hit” had gone 10 feet in the air. But the next Miami hitter compensated for that distance disparity with a 400-foot home run.

George Solomon, the Washington Post's great sports editor for 28 years, emailed me: “Nats ninth inning performance Sunday as low as you can get.”

When a team blows its 35th save of the year, and the blown-save record, at least for this solar system, is only 37, a fan learns to root in the fetal position.

On a roller-coaster homestand as crazy as this, even rookie managers with cherubic faces get crusty. After one lazy 13-1 loss, Blake Butera publicly threw his team under the bus — where they deserved to be. His accusation of “lack of energy” is one step from “quit.”

Twice, Butera relieved Jake Irvin in the fifth inning before he was eligible for a win. It was the percentage move. Vets seldom like that; good managers don’t care. Butera also yanked Jorbit Vivas out mid-game for not running out a pop up. It would have been a waste for this season to be so cuddly that a ticked-off Butera never showed up.
Blake Butera (5702x3801, AR: 1.50)In other sports, devoted fans may wait a week for real news, or at least a few days. In MLB, the full range of a team’s possible futures rush at you constantly.

For example, with his current torrid streak, Lile now has a career OPS+ — OPS adjusted for era and home park — of 115, or 15% better than league average, in 929 plate appearances. Lile isn’t James Wood: 136! But 115 is in the same neighborhood as Ryan Zimmerman, Adrian Beltré, Roberto Alomar, Barry Larkin, Mickey Vernon, Thurman Munson and Byron Buxton. And Lile is only 23.

Counterbalancing that, Crews now has a .215 batting average in more than 800 plate appearances. After his walk-off hit, teammates pounded his back with joy because he’s such a hard-working, hard-nosed but hard-on-himself player who expects greatness — not mere goodness, much less mediocrity — from himself.

Take a deep breath. The average No. 2 overall draft pick has a career WAR of 15.2, not 50.0, and, if he’s an outfielder like Crews, a career average of 199 homers, not 500.

Useful centerfielder B.J. Upton (16.5 WAR, 168 homers), who was never an All-Star, is a fair measuring stick for a player in Crews’ draft slot, not Reggie Jackson. Crews has climbing to do, but reaching the top of a hill, not an Alp, might suffice.

As this season winds down, let’s step back. In recent years, the Nats have been almost unwatchable, even for a lunatic like me. This year, the fact that a late-season homestand could be engrossing proves how much progress the Paul Toboni regime has made.

You play for the scoreboard every day. But, over a season, your run differential tells plenty of truth, too. In ’26, the Nats have improved from -214 (awful) to +14 (average). That’s enormous.

Once a team becomes competitive again, as the Nats have, the sport regains its power to please. In one homestand near the end of a typical season for a typical team, so many remarkable things happen that a MLB fan can hardly believe it all, pulling out hair one night, but waking up smiling after the next game.

It’s 13-3 your way one night and a 13-1 loss two days later. This whole Nats homestand was a useful 6-4, with plenty of young players to ponder for the future. But in the final game Wednesday, the first-place Braves, kicked the previous night by those rookies, kicked back with a 9-0 win. The Nats got two hits.

After many years, you know this is how it goes. You internalize a coping mechanism for loss and an endless anticipation of hope. That sounds like daily existence. Recuperate and repeat. For a lifetime.

entries.title: Rep. Nikki Budzinski Announces a Bid to Chair the New Democrat Coalition
entries.summary: The Illinois representative wants to lead the centrist group as a slate of progressives are expected to enter Congress next year.
entries.content:
Rep. Nikki Budzinski wants to lead the centrist New Democrat Coalition next year, coinciding with an expected incoming wave of new House progressives hoping to expand the chamber’s left flank.

“I am confident I can lead us into what will be a consequential next chapter,” Budzinski said in a “Dear Colleague” letter seeking the group’s chairmanship, shared first with NOTUS.

Budzinski, a moderate who currently serves as the coalition’s vice chair of policy, is the first Democrat to throw her hat in the ring for the position.

With the likely arrival of a slate of new left-wing House Democrats, the party’s largest ideological caucus could face an uphill battle getting centrist priorities past the finish line even if Democrats win back the majority in November. Whoever chairs the group next year would need to balance potential conflicts between the party’s centrist and progressive wings.

In June, the group’s current chair, Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Illinois), waved away concerns about the way party priorities might shift next year.

“We’re not going to change who we are and what we’re fighting for,” Schneider, who is term-limited, told reporters. “You only do things by building a coalition, getting 218 votes. … Much of the legislative ideas we have put forth in the past and are proposing in the future are ideas that build coalitions that cross party lines.”

In her letter, Budzinski pointed to the party’s recent “commitment to pragmatic progress” and touted her work “toward building the largest majority possible.” The Illinois representative referenced her raising $2.5 million for House Democrats’ campaign arm this cycle and nearly $700,000 in direct contributions to “Red to Blue” candidates endorsed by the New Democrat Coalition’s political operation.

“Nikki has been a true leader who knows how to build a strong coalition that knows how to accomplish an agenda that moves this country forward,” Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nevada), a coalition member, told NOTUS. “She understands that in order for Democrats to hold a majority in Congress we must deliver results. I believe she will help do that.”

The elections for the New Democrat Coalition’s leadership for next the Congress will take place in November during new member orientation. It’s unclear if other lawmakers are considering running, but only current and former vice chairs can do so. Rep. Ami Bera (D-California), a former vice chair, previously considered a bid but his office confirmed he will not be running for next cycle.

entries.title: Maine Labor Day Rally Nixes Its Planned Graham Platner Speech
entries.summary: Platner had been scheduled to speak Monday at the rally in Ellsworth.
entries.content:
By Patrick Whittle

PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Former Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner is no longer set to speak at a Labor Day rally when he makes his first major public appearance since ending his campaign against Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine.

Platner, who won the nomination in June but dropped out in July after Politico reported that a former girlfriend said he sexually assaulted her, had been scheduled to speak Monday at the rally in Ellsworth, near his hometown of Sullivan. He has denied the allegations.

Platner was expected to speak about labor history and the importance of unions in the U.S. Event organizers were urged not to let him speak by the former girlfriend and another woman who has accused him of domestic abuse.

Organizers said Wednesday that the planned speech was drawing negative media attention, and he will instead lead a veterans' march after the rally.

“Graham is not speaking,” said Carol Leonard of Hancock County Activists, a progressive group organizing the rally. “The media frenzy got just too insane, and we became concerned about safety.”

Platner is an oyster farmer and combat veteran who filled theaters around Maine during a barnstorming campaign that resulted in a decisive win over Gov. Janet Mills, who suspended her campaign before the primary.

He has no experience in elected office but fashioned a campaign focused on working-class issues such as the high costs of housing and healthcare.

Platner’s campaign was frequently interrupted by scandals, such as the emergence in late May of media reports that he previously exchanged sexually explicit text messages with several women while he was married.

High-profile backers including independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders stood by him in the wake of those allegations, but his support crumbled after the sexual assault allegations surfaced.

Platner also had a tattoo recognized as a Nazi symbol, though he said he did not realize its association with Nazism until he was several weeks into the campaign. He later had the tattoo covered up with a different design.

Platner also apologized for old online comments that included insulting language about women, police and rural residents.

After he dropped out of the race, Democrats held a nominating convention in July in which they chose former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson to run against Collins.

Jackson, who got the Senate nomination after losing a gubernatorial primary, campaigned with Platner in the spring but has distanced himself from him following the sexual assault allegations.

The Ellsworth event is scheduled for midday and will include speakers, live music and the veterans' march.
